Over the past decade, one of the most fascinating observations in the world of precious metals has been the bizarre decoupling in the supply/demand dynamics and thus pricing, between paper and physical gold.

As gold became increasingly financialized in recent years - through futures, ETFs, derivatives and so on - and as the impact of "financialized" gold became the dominant price-setting factor in a world where the nominal volume of "paper gold" traded is now orders of magnitude greater than "physical", a bizarre decoupling emerges every time there is a major market stress event. A pattern that has emerged is that during periods of "bathwater" liquidation, when levered asset managers are forced to dump paper gold to cover margin calls in different parts of their book, sending the price of gold sharply lower also happens to be when physical gold buyers step up amid concerns over the viability of either the financial system and/or the reserve currency.

I wrote this out for another verse and thought I'd repost it here - just some simple stew recipes. Shout if you want more detail.

I use a dutch oven or a stovetop pot for most of my stews.

Tomorrow I am stewing some sirloin of beef I have in the freezer, if it's defrosted. This is just browned onions, chopped salted meat browned in the onions with herbs, then I add in veggies (not too many to keep it meaty, probably some carrots, a parsnip or two if I can get them, and some mushrooms, hopefully portabello). Add a bay leaf for flavor.

I just add all the veg to the meat and onions with a can of tomatoes, some tomato puree, herbs, stock (highly recommend a brand called Better than Boullion) and some red wine and worcester sauce.

--

If you're worried about getting the virus and want a bit of an immune booster; chicken stew from thighs and legs is great. Onions, LOTS Of garlic, brown the meat, add in some carrots, mushrooms, courgette, lots of black pepper, white wine, then when it is ready to serve add some fresh chopped parsley. Parsley is extremely easy to keep in a pot and it's great for the immune system (and a delicious finisher to soups and chicken stews). When the chicken is falling from the bone, take out all the bones (just ladle it up and pull them out - it REALLY helps if you can remember how many pieces you put in and how many bones you are expecting).

--

Another nice one, very simple - goulash (one version of it, at least). Just onions, salted and peppered, fried, brown some nice cubed beef, a good stewing cut, then add tinned tomatoes, puree, a couple of bay leaves, a dash of paprika, then cook until the beef is tender - in a normal oven you want to give it 3 hours.

--
